opus-5.5.text:
Well, I don't think there's actually a tension there; I think they're two sides of the same coin. People often set up emergence and fundamental principles as if they were opposites: either everything is reducible to a few simple laws, or there's this mysterious new stuff that appears at higher levels. But if you look at how physics actually works, symmetries are what give you the laws at each level, and emergence is what happens when those symmetries get broken, or when new effective symmetries appear at a larger scale.

Take a simple example. The fundamental laws of physics are rotationally symmetric, but a crystal isn't. The crystal picks out particular directions. That's spontaneous symmetry breaking, and it's precisely where a lot of the interesting emergent structure comes from. Phase transitions, magnetism, even the Higgs mechanism: these are all stories about symmetries at one level giving rise to qualitatively new behavior at another. Phil Anderson's "More Is Different" paper is essentially an argument built on that idea. So emergence isn't the absence of symmetry; it's what symmetry does when you go up in scale.

And then at the higher level you often discover new symmetries that weren't obvious from below. Fluid dynamics has its own invariances that you would never guess from staring at the Schrödinger equation. Renormalization is basically the mathematics of how the effective description, including its symmetries, changes as you change scale. So the picture I have in mind is a hierarchy of levels, each with its own symmetries, connected by breaking and coarse-graining.

Now, why does this matter for AI? Because I think learning is, to a large degree, the discovery of symmetries. When a convolutional network works, it's because it builds in translation invariance. Graph neural networks build in permutation invariance. The whole geometric deep learning program is about this. But the deeper point is that we shouldn't have to hand-code all the symmetries; a really good learner should discover them from data, including the emergent ones that only show up at higher levels of abstraction. That's a big part of what intelligence is: finding the invariances in the world that let you compress it and generalize from it.

And that connects to emergence in the learning system itself. The capabilities people describe as emergent in large models, I'd argue, are often the system latching onto a symmetry or structure in the data that it couldn't represent before. It looks like a sudden jump, but underneath there's a structure being picked up.

So my view is: symmetry is the grammar, emergence is the poetry. You can't have the poetry without the grammar, but you also can't predict the poem just from knowing the grammar. And the job of a master algorithm, if we ever get one, is to learn both: the invariances at each level and how the levels relate to each other.

r001.rationale: The response says emergence occurs when underlying symmetries are broken and illustrates this with a crystal, whose structure arises through spontaneous symmetry breaking.

r002.rationale: It discusses laws and symmetry changes across scales, but does not attribute laws’ limited usefulness for higher-level phenomena to symmetry breakings inherited from the universe’s beginning.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize evolution as a succession of spontaneous symmetry breakings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I don't actually think there's a tension there, and I think the reason people see one is that they're using "emergence" in a slightly mystical sense. When I talk about emergence, I just mean that you have a system whose components follow simple rules, and the behavior of the whole is something you couldn't have easily predicted by staring at the components. The behavior of a market, the behavior of a brain, the behavior of a large neural network. None of that violates the underlying rules. It's just that the mapping from the rules to the macro behavior is complicated.

Symmetry is on the other side of that same coin. A symmetry is a statement about what doesn't change when you transform something. In physics, you get conservation laws from symmetries through Noether's theorem. In machine learning, the whole reason convolutional networks work is translation symmetry: a cat is a cat whether it's in the top left or the bottom right of the image. Transformers get you permutation symmetry over the input, graph neural networks get you symmetry over node relabelings. The symmetry is what makes learning tractable, because it collapses an enormous hypothesis space down to something you can actually fit with finite data.

So here's how they fit together. Symmetries are the constraints, the invariances that the system has to respect. Emergence is what happens inside the space those constraints leave open. The symmetries don't determine what the system does, they determine what it can't do, and then the dynamics fill in the rest. If you look at something like a Hopfield network or a modern LLM, you've got a few very simple symmetric operations, repeated at scale, and out of that you get behaviors that nobody wrote down, that nobody designed. That's emergence sitting right on top of symmetry.

And frankly, I think this is the most interesting frontier for the field. The deep learning people have been very good at exploiting symmetries empirically, more or less by trial and error. What we don't have yet is a theory that tells you which symmetries you should build in, which ones the system should discover for itself, and what emerges when you let it do that. That, to me, is a big chunk of what a master algorithm would have to get right.

r001.rationale: The response says emergence does not violate underlying rules and describes symmetries as constraints, but it does not identify spontaneous symmetry breaking as a mechanism for emergence.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss the history of spontaneous symmetry breakings, the beginning of the universe, or how that history limits physical laws' explanations of higher-level phenomena.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize evolution as a succession of spontaneous symmetry breakings.

astra-6.text:
I don’t see a contradiction there. Symmetry is about what stays the same when something changes, and emergence is about what happens when you put a lot of interacting components together. You can have very simple rules, with very strong symmetries, and still get extraordinarily complex behavior out of them.

Think about a cellular automaton. The same rule applies at every location, so there’s a symmetry built into the system. But the patterns that emerge can be very complicated. The symmetry of the rule doesn’t mean that every configuration has to look the same.

And in machine learning, that connection is very useful. Learning is partly about discovering what you can ignore—what transformations leave the thing you care about unchanged. An object is still the same object when it moves across an image. Capturing that invariance helps you generalize. But when you combine many learned representations, you can get capabilities that aren’t obvious from looking at any one component.

So symmetries constrain what can happen; they don’t give you an immediate description of everything that will happen. That leaves plenty of room for emergence.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t see those as contradictory. Symmetry is about what stays the same when you change something, while emergence is about what happens when you put things together. The rules governing the parts can have very simple symmetries, and yet the collective behavior can be extraordinarily rich.

Think about symmetry breaking. The underlying rules don’t necessarily pick out a particular direction or configuration, but the system settles into one. So having symmetric laws doesn’t mean that everything those laws produce has to look symmetric.

In machine learning, we build in symmetries because they help us generalize. If you move a cat to another part of an image, it’s still a cat. But that constraint doesn’t tell you everything the model will learn, or what capabilities will arise from combining many learned features.

The important distinction, I think, is between emergence as something we didn’t anticipate and emergence as something that somehow escapes the underlying rules. The first is everywhere. The second is a much stronger claim, and you don’t need it to explain why simple principles can produce very surprising intelligence.

r001.rationale: It explains that symmetric underlying rules can yield emergent behavior when a system settles into a particular configuration through symmetry breaking.

r002.rationale: It does not connect the limited explanatory usefulness of physical laws for higher-level phenomena to a history of symmetry breakings inherited from the universe’s beginning.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize evolution as a succession of spontaneous symmetry breakings.
